nameStory: This tall sunflower is named after Prince Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied, a German explorer and naturalist who encountered it during his famous journey through the American frontier in the 1830s. The prince was documenting the plants and wildlife of the Great Plains, and this towering sunflower made such an impression that botanists honored him by giving it his name.
description: Maximilian sunflower is a towering prairie giant that can reach 6-10 feet tall, making it one of our most impressive wildflowers. It produces clusters of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers along its upper stems in late summer and fall. This is actually a Great Plains native that has naturalized in parts of New England, bringing a taste of the western prairies to our region. Unlike the giant garden sunflowers you might know, this species has many smaller flower heads rather than one enormous bloom.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely tall plant reaching 6-10 feet, often towering above most other wildflowers with a sturdy, unbranched main stem that feels rough to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Multiple bright yellow flower heads clustered along the upper portion of the stem, each about 2-3 inches across with 10-20 narrow petals surrounding a dark center disk

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves that feel sandpaper-rough and are arranged alternately up the stem, often folding slightly along the midrib and giving off a faint sunflower scent when crushed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark sunflower seeds with fluffy white bristles that catch the wind, produced in abundance from the flower centers in fall

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stems that feel rough and hairy, often reddish-tinged near the base and sometimes developing a woody texture by late season

habitat: In New England, look for Maximilian sunflower in sunny, open areas like old fields, roadsides, and disturbed sites where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often appearing along fence rows or in areas where prairie plants have been planted for restoration or ornamental purposes.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge as clusters of rough, sandpapery leaves close to the ground, growing rapidly once warm weather arrives.
seasonality.summer: Plants shoot skyward, developing their characteristic towering height and rough-textured foliage throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming occurs from August through October, when the tall stems are crowned with clusters of bright yellow flowers that attract butterflies and bees.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems often persist through winter as tall, brown stalks topped with empty seed heads that provide food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

funFact: This prairie powerhouse can live for decades and develops a massive underground root system that can extend 15 feet deep, making it incredibly drought-tolerant and allowing it to access water that most other plants can't reach.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tall sunflowers, but Maximilian sunflower's extreme height, narrow leaves, and multiple flower clusters distinguish it from shorter species like woodland sunflower. Remember: "Max is maximum height" - if it's towering 8+ feet tall with clusters of sunflowers, think Maximilian.
contextualKnowledge: Though native to the Great Plains, this species has been widely planted as an ornamental and for wildlife habitat restoration, which is how it arrived in New England. It's sometimes called "prairie sunflower" and represents one of nature's most successful examples of westward-to-eastward plant migration.
compareHints: Among New England's sunflowers, Maximilian stands out for its exceptional height - much taller than woodland sunflower or Jerusalem artichoke. While giant sunflower can also get quite tall, Maximilian has narrower leaves and tends to bloom later in the season. Its multiple flower clusters also distinguish it from common sunflower, which typically has one large flower head per stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woodland sunflower stands out from its sunflower relatives by its distinctly rough stem texture and preference for partial shade.
Among New England sunflowers, Jerusalem artichoke stands out for its late fall blooming time and extremely rough leaf texture.

Common sunflower dwarfs its New England relatives in size - while woodland sunflower and Jerusalem artichoke typically stay under 6 feet with smaller flower heads, common sunflower towers above them with flower heads that can be 6-12 inches across.
Among New England's sunflowers, pale sunflower stands out for its notably light-colored petals and preference for partial shade.
Giant sunflower stands out from its sunflower relatives by being the tallest and preferring wetland habitats, while most other Helianthus species favor drier ground.
Among New England sunflowers, ashy sunflower is unique for its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves – all the others like woodland sunflower and Jerusalem artichoke have much smoother, greener foliage.

Among New England's sunflowers, pale-leaved woodland sunflower is distinguished by its whitish leaf undersides, while woodland sunflower has green undersides and Jerusalem artichoke grows much taller with broader leaves.

Stiff sunflower differs from other New England sunflowers by having most of its rough, sandpapery leaves clustered near the base rather than distributed evenly up the stem like woodland sunflower or giant sunflower.
